qa.q: Maria: How should I be confident in my IELTS speaking?
qa.a: Because you get nervous, it's an exam. You enter this room, the examiner is looking at you, and you're starting trembling, you're nervous.
Rory: Maybe we should share what we do to boost our confidence first.
Rory: I work on breathing a lot, like deep breaths, calm down.

qa.q: Do you do anything like that, breathing?
qa.a: Maria: Absolutely. I think breathing helps a lot. I used to do quite a lot of speaking in public, presenting stuff about IELTS. Now I train teachers and I do get nervous. So before my presentation, I'm just in an office or somewhere in the corridor, so I take three deep breaths. Really deep.

qa.q: Rory: Is it in through the mouth, out through the nose or is that not important?
qa.a: Maria: I think it doesn't matter through the nose, through the mouth, but you should breathe from your belly. Really deep, not just like, no, but like really one, two, three, four, and still breathing in. And then breathe out. When you are breathing out, it can be even longer. Rory: That's true. I can remember reading something that you should never breathe from your chest in order to calm down. You can tell when people are agitated because their chest goes, not their stomach. Maria: Actually, it doesn't matter from your chest, from your belly, or both, from your belly and then from your chest. Just take three deep breaths and maybe count to five, like one, two, three, four, five.

Or breathing in. So that helps to relax your body. Rory: So that works in the immediate term, probably remembering that it's an exam, it's not life and death. The exam's important, but if you don't do so well, you can recover.

qa.q: One way of thinking about this is like, how am I going to feel about this in five years' time?
qa.a: There are very few things in life people can't recover from. Failing an exam is something that you can always recover from. You just have to take the test again. If that's what's needed, then that's what's needed. So two things in the immediate term.

qa.q: Anything in the long term that can be done?
qa.a: Maria: Preparation. So preparation does boost your confidence, especially about speaking.

qa.q: You can check out the topics, right?
qa.a: On this podcast, we've been discussing pretty much all the current topics. Rory: We have, and I think that we've done a good job of preparing people. A lot of teachers that are not us are working on that as well. So it's important to realize that preparing in advance and the role of that plays is quite important.

qa.q: Maria: If you haven't prepared in advance, at least read about the format of the speaking, right?
qa.a: So that it has three parts, and there's an examiner, it's recorded.

qa.q: So knowing the format of the speaking and some topics, still, it gives you some confidence, right?
qa.a: So you know what to expect. Rory: Exactly. So I think that's important for exams in general. I mention this every single time I present about this exam and exams in general, but I'll say this again because some teachers listen to us. If your students are preparing for IELTS, please show them the exam. So like, download the sample papers, show the students the different parts of the reading, and the writing, and the listening, and the speaking. Watch videos that show how the speaking goes, because they're there, it's all online. Maria: There are videos of the speaking exam. Rory: Because it's really frustrating when you see people coming into exams and they don't know what's required of them. That's the teacher's job. So it's something that's super important and it's not a waste of time at all. You might not be teaching them any vocabulary, but you are teaching them something that's really important. So it's good to do. I did a bit of research. Maria: Oh. Rory: Yes, and I should say, not all of this is my own, so I should cite my sources beforehand. I listened to a YouTuber called Katie Morton. She does a lot of work with mental health. One thing that she did recently was four tips on how to boost your confidence. So I thought we could talk about that for a little bit. The first thing that she said was, you need to have a clear idea of what your strengths are. She was talking about it in the context of dating.

qa.q: But actually, we could change this to think like, what can I speak well about?
qa.a: So you know for a fact that in my case, I can't speak about conditional sentences. So I don't. And I let Maria do that. But I can speak quite well about collocations, for example, and the use of tenses to convey meaning. So this is something that I do. In the case of people preparing for the exam, think, well, I'm not very good at storytelling, but I can answer questions about things. I'm good at talking about things that are familiar to me. Connected to that is, once you know what you're good at, then you work out what you're bad at, and then you just practice, practice, practice as much as you possibly can. This is where your teacher comes in. If you have a teacher, they should help you identify these strengths and weaknesses as well. And the other thing is, when you work out what your strengths are, you accept what your limitations are, and then you ask questions and do the research in order to address these problems. If they are in fact problems, just because you can't answer all of the topics on part one perfectly, doesn't mean to say that you're lost. You have time to recover in part two. That's a time when you can prepare your answer and you brainstorm all of this vocabulary that you know. And then the other side of that is it's not just a mental thing, but it's also a physical thing as well. It's not a case of dressing in a certain way for other people, but dressing for yourself. If you feel confident about how you look, that also boosts your confidence in general. So if you dress nicely, then you feel good about yourself. I should say, these things work together. It's not just a case of, put on a nice shirt and all of your problems will be solved. You need to do all of these things in equal measure, and that can really help boost your confidence in general, but if we talk about for exams then it's good to. Maria: Yes, I like that one. And another thing that Katie Morton was talking about is stopping negative self-talk. Wow, that's a nice one. Rory: Some people, and students in particular, this is extremely frustrating. It's understandable why it happens. But some people in particular say the most awful things about themselves. Like I was teaching in Don Jada a couple of weeks ago, and this woman was saying like, "Oh, I'm retarded, I can't do anything properly in English." That's really upsetting.

qa.q: You need to stop this and think like, "Okay, I can't do this, but what can I do?
qa.a: " And then move from there. So don't say horrible things about yourself. It's not just words. The things that you express about yourself actually do have an impact on your self-image. Maria: Thoughts are material. Rory: Exactly. And connected to this, the opposite is actually helpful. This is another thing that Katie Morton was saying is, start putting positivity out into the world. Not just about yourself, not just saying nice things about yourself, but nice things about other people or just things that happen in general. One thing I like to do is send people nice comments on Instagram when I see their stories and just say like, "That's a really cool thing that you did, good for you." Maria: Praise people for something. Rory: Exactly. You'll get that back. That makes you feel better yourself, because you have done something to help make that person stay better. I think that can be quite good. And then the other side of that is, it's not just a mental thing, but it's also a physical thing as well. It's not a case of dressing in a certain way for other people, but dressing for yourself. If you feel confident about how you look, that also boosts your confidence in general. So if you dress nicely, then you feel good about yourself. I should say, these things work together. It's not just a case of, put on a nice shirt and all of your problems will be solved. You need to do all of these things in equal measure, and that can really help boost your confidence in general, but if we talk about for exams then it's good to. Maria: Put on something with your favorite color, or put your favorite pair of jeans or trainers. It doesn't matter if it's smart or casual, but something like you feel you look good, you look more than good, you look gorgeous, like people look at you, they notice you. It doesn't matter what the clothes are, but you feel confident in this particular jacket.

qa.q: For example, I train teachers and usually most teachers are much older than me, and I look young, right?
qa.a: And here I am looking like a 14-year-old, 16, or maybe 20.

qa.q: And then these teachers they look at me like, "Who are you?
qa.a: " And to avoid this, I put on my best shoes ever and I put on my best dress and I look like, "Wow" in the shoes and the dress. And this does make an impact on people. Because again, I'm confident. I'm not just standing in the corner like, "Hello, I'm Maria." No, I look confident. I'm projecting this confidence. I have powerful body language. I smile, but again, I look natural. And they feel it. They look at my appearance. They take it in, my body language, my confidence, my colors, clothes. And pretty much most of them comment on the shoes later. And again, some people tell me that, "Oh, I was scared of you," kind of. And because of this confidence, because of this power that you're projecting. And clothes are important. Rory: It works in the same way for men as well. We could talk about being dressed well, but we talk about dressing professionally in particular. Men wear suits because this is, it's like a military uniform almost. And that puts you in that mindset of being professional, I'm in control of the situation. So there is a great deal of psychology in play based upon how you look. It's not the only thing that counts. You have to know your stuff. This is why we led in with like, practice, practice, practice. Work on the inside first, and then the outside. Maria and I know a lot about fashion. Maria: Oh. Rory: Obviously we're going to play to our strengths.

qa.q: Maria: You should feel comfortable, right?
Another point is when you do feel nervous and you look at the examiner, imagine this examiner in the bathroom. Rory: What?
qa.a: Maria: Yes, like you imagine the person next to you or in front of you. And when you're nervous because of this person, this person makes you nervous. So imagine them like a normal, a usual human being in the bathroom. Rory: Well, they are. Maria: They are, like the same as you. It's not something like even if you're standing in front of a president, it's a person. Rory: They want you to succeed as well. There's nobody in that room that doesn't want you to do well. And on top of that, they're probably quite nervous too. I don't think a lot of people appreciate the fact that examiners do have strict procedures to follow. Maria: Yeah. Rory: So it's not just you in that room that's terrified. It's the both of you. And you have to work together somehow to make this process work. Maria: You can make the examiner nervous with your beautiful clothes and your gorgeous English. Rory: They probably do. They probably are quite nervous. So just acknowledge that no one's out there to get you. Everybody wants you to win. Maria: Even if the examiner doesn't smile, if you feel that the examiner looks gloomy and very serious, or it's because you said something wrong. No, the examiner is doing their job. The examiner is being monitored quite frequently. Cambridge checks the examiners. Rory: Exactly. That's the thing, you'll notice when you go into that exam room, there's a recorder in front of the examiner. So their supervisor hears everything that happens in that room. Maria: They are under pressure. Rory: They are under pressure. It's probably, we can come back to our original point that we made, that you can recover from failure. So say that you don't get the result that you want, you can appeal that. The reason you can appeal that is because every single IELTS speaking test is recorded. So don't just think, just because I've got this result, I have to accept it. You don't.

qa.q: You can challenge it, and you should, absolutely. So why not?
qa.a: Maria: If you feel that the examiner interrupted you, the examiner disagreed with your opinions and said, "No, it's wrong." If, for example, the speaking exam was less than 11 minutes, because the official timing is from 11 to 14 minutes. If your speaking exam was eight minutes, you should appeal. You should complain. Rory: If your speaking exam was 11 minutes, you should still appeal. You should give people the maximum amount of time to express themselves. If you haven't, especially if you want to say more, and you haven't been given that chance, then definitely appeal. Maria: And if again, you disagree with the results, you can appeal. There's this procedure, and on our Instagram there's a video with me talking about the procedure, because there are certain deadlines and you fill in this special form and then your speaking result gets rechecked. Rory: Exactly. They can't lower your score. So it's either stays the same or they can give you a higher score, but they can't lower the score. Maria: Okay, so we talked about breathing, so take three deep breaths right before you enter this speaking exam room. Then prepare. We talked about preparation, so know the format, know the topics, write down some nice vocabulary and grammar you want to use.

qa.q: Rory, you talked about the tips, so could you sum up the tips?
qa.a: Rory: I suppose the best way of doing it is, know your strengths, practice those until they improve, know your weaknesses, work out how to improve them, and practice those. Be beautiful on the inside and be beautiful on the outside. On the subject of all of these things, find somebody to practice with. It can be a friend, but I think the person that will help you the most with this is a teacher. So with that in mind, get yourself a teacher. If you can't afford a teacher, we have a speaking partners group that helps people to prepare for this. It's not as professional as a teacher, obviously, but you can still meet like-minded people and work towards a goal together. The final thing is, if you've got any questions that you'd like to have answered and maybe you can't afford a teacher, then you can always drop me a line on Instagram, and I don't mind answering any questions that people might have, because it's scary. Sometimes it can be nice and reassuring if somebody's there to say, "Okay, this is fine, let's talk about how to fix it." Maria: Success with IELTS Instagram and Telegram, and the chat where you can find a speaking partner for free, that's on our Telegram. Everything is available on our premium, because if you invest into our premium, you get the speaking course, you get some webinars, so you get support, check out our premium. And again, as Rory has told you, just drop us a line on Instagram, on social media. Rory: I think that wraps up the confidence part nicely. Maria: Thank you very much for your attention, time, and support. Good luck with your exams when they come, and remember, confidence is key.

vocab.e: What should you do to boost your confidence?

preparing in advance is quite important.

To project positive energy or thoughts into the world.
vocab.e: start putting positivity out into the world.

vocab.e: If you feel confident about how you look, you feel good about yourself.

vocab.d: Non-verbal communication that conveys strength and confidence.
